title: Automate your invoice bookkeeping
description: A system that reads each vendor invoice as it arrives and drafts a journal entry for you to approve before it posts.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

workflow.title: Workflow
workflow.content: A multi-step process Claude runs to accomplish a goal — for example: read emails → filter by topic → summarize → post to Slack. Workflows can be run manually or on a schedule.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

routing-pattern.title: Routing (Orchestration Pattern)
routing-pattern.content: An orchestration pattern where a classifier looks at the input and sends it down a specialized path — support tickets to the refund flow, bug reports to the triage flow. Each path stays simple because it only handles its own kind of input.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: A vendor invoice takes 9.2 days to process industry-wide and costs $9.40, versus 3.1 days and $2.78 at the best-in-class accounts payable teams, per [Ardent Partners's Accounts Payable Metrics That Matter in 2025](https://ardentpartners.com/ap-metrics-that-matter-in-2025/). Touchless processing sits at 32.6% industry average against 49.2% for best-in-class teams, per the same report.

Every time a vendor invoice arrives, by email or upload, this system pulls the vendor name, invoice number, dates, line items, and total, then drafts a journal entry against your chart of accounts. The entry sits in a queue labeled pending review until an accountant signs off. Anything missing, unreadable, or that looks like a duplicate gets flagged instead of guessed at.

It runs as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) each time an invoice lands, a saved skill for whoever processes them daily, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) watching an inbox or shared folder. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your ledger.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a scope naming how invoices arrive, the fields you need extracted, your journal entry format, and who approves entries before they post.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that extracts data from vendor invoices and drafts journal entries for my review. Ask me questions, one at a time, about how invoices arrive today, what fields I need extracted, what my journal entry format and account structure look like, who approves entries before they post, and what should trigger a manual hold instead of a draft. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to define your account structure and hold rules before any invoice touches the system.

items: How invoices arrive (email inbox, shared drive, vendor portal), and whether that needs a [routing](#tooltip-routing-pattern) step first.
Where your chart of accounts and vendor history live, so the model has real categorization rules to work from.
Who has final sign-off before an entry posts, and what your hold process looks like for exceptions.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather what it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are your accounting or ERP system (QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite), an OCR or document intake tool for reading the invoice, and your approval [workflow](#tooltip-workflow), whether that's email, [Slack](#tooltip-slack), or the accounting system's own review queue. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real invoice, PDF or image. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Extract the key data from this invoice and draft a journal entry for review.

Context: Invoice attached (PDF or image). My journal entry format uses these accounts: [paste your relevant GL accounts]. This vendor has historically been coded to [account/category], if that helps.

Rules: Extract vendor name, invoice number, invoice date, due date, line items, and total. Draft a journal entry using only accounts from my chart of accounts, never invent one. If any required field is missing, unreadable, or the invoice looks like a duplicate of one already processed, flag it and do not draft an entry. Every draft entry must be labeled "pending review," never "posted."

Output format: A structured summary of extracted fields, followed by the draft journal entry in debit/credit format, followed by a flags section noting anything uncertain or missing.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the "pending review" label and the flag-instead-of-guess rule keep a missing field or a duplicate charge from turning into a silent posting error.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every field extracted, entries labeled pending review, duplicates and missing data flagged?
**Feedback.** Tell it what went wrong, a GL code that doesn't exist, a duplicate it missed, and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Build a vendor spend summary that runs alongside the pipeline.
Add an automatic three-way match against purchase orders and receiving records.
Extend it to flag unusual price changes from a recurring vendor.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric), not a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each draft journal entry, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, invoice source, fields extracted correctly, entries flagged instead of drafted, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a recurring extraction error visible after a week of entries.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few weeks straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. OCR and extraction will occasionally misread a number or duplicate a vendor's charge. Treat the held-for-review queue as the safety mechanism, and never let a draft entry post on its own.
